name: Cortex
tagline: A personal knowledge tool for capturing notes and linking them into something you can actually navigate later.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core of a linked-notes app is not hard: markdown files on disk, wiki-style links, backlinks, full text search, maybe a graph view. An agent can produce that in a sitting and it will feel surprisingly good for a week. What breaks is everything around the edges: sync across devices, a mobile capture path, editor polish, and the thousand small keyboard and rendering behaviors that make a notes app feel like a tool instead of a demo. Any AI features layered on top mean you are now paying an API bill and writing prompt plumbing yourself. Worth building if you want to own the files, which is a real reason; not worth building if you mostly wanted a nicer editor.
coreLoopDIY: Runs a local web app over a folder of markdown files with wiki-links, live backlinks, full text search, and a clickable graph of connections.
requirements: Node 20+ and a local folder to use as the vault
Optional OpenAI or Anthropic API key if you want summaries or auto-linking suggestions
Something like Syncthing, Dropbox, or a git repo if you want the vault on more than one machine
whatYouLose: Mobile apps and quick capture from a phone
Hosted sync and conflict resolution that someone else debugged
Editor polish: paste handling, tables, images, undo that behaves
Any built in AI features, unless you wire and pay for them yourself
Someone else maintaining it when a dependency breaks in six months
moatNotes: Notes apps live and die on typing feel and trust that nothing gets lost. Neither shows up in a feature list, both show up on day thirty.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for notes tools because the thing they want is not features, it is confidence: that capture is one tap away on any device, that sync will not eat a paragraph, and that the editor will not fight them mid thought. A weekend build can match the data model exactly and still lose on all three. The other half of it is that the alternative to paying is maintaining your own writing environment forever, which is a fun hobby right up until you have a deadline.
notes: Owning plain markdown files is the actual win here, and you can have that without building anything at all.
prompt:
Build a local personal knowledge base web app that reads and writes plain markdown files in a folder on disk. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Node 20 with Express and TypeScript for the backend
- React with Vite and TypeScript for the frontend
- better-sqlite3 with FTS5 for the search index, stored in .cortex/index.db inside the vault
- CodeMirror 6 for the editor
- d3-force for the graph view

Behavior:
- Vault path comes from VAULT_DIR in .env. Create .env.example, never hardcode paths.
- Markdown files are the source of truth. The SQLite index is disposable and rebuildable.
- On boot, walk the vault, parse YAML frontmatter, extract [[wiki links]] and #tags, build the index. Watch the folder with chokidar and reindex changed files.
- Left pane: file tree plus a search box. Search hits FTS5 and shows snippets with matches highlighted.
- Center pane: CodeMirror editor with markdown syntax highlighting, autosave 800ms after typing stops, and autocomplete on [[ that suggests existing note titles.
- Right pane: backlinks list for the current note, plus outgoing links and tags.
- /graph route: force directed graph of notes as nodes and wiki links as edges, click a node to open that note.
- Ctrl/Cmd+K opens a quick switcher that fuzzy matches note titles and creates the note if it does not exist.
- Clicking a [[link]] to a missing note creates it with frontmatter containing title and created date.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile apps, sync, multi user, sharing, AI features, WYSIWYG rendering, plugin system.

Deliver a README with setup steps, a single npm run dev that starts both server and client, and a npm run reindex script that rebuilds the index from scratch. Include a smoke test that creates two notes, links them, and asserts the backlink appears.
